title: Relation Logic
purpose: Seed the formal properties of relations so Lantern preserves argument roles and only performs inversion, symmetry, transitivity or composition when those operations are explicitly licensed.

concepts.definition: A predicate whose ordered argument positions connect two or more terms.
A relation with two ordered argument positions, conventionally R(a,b).
The semantic position occupied by an argument; exchanging roles can change the proposition.
Relation S is the inverse of R when R(a,b) holds exactly when S(b,a) holds under the declared semantics.
R is symmetric when R(a,b) implies R(b,a).
R is asymmetric when R(a,b) implies NOT R(b,a).
R is antisymmetric when R(a,b) and R(b,a) together imply a=b.
R is transitive when R(a,b) and R(b,c) imply R(a,c).
R is intransitive when R(a,b) and R(b,c) imply NOT R(a,c) where the definition applies.
A relation lacking a transitivity declaration licenses neither R(a,c) nor NOT R(a,c) from a two-edge chain.
R is reflexive on domain D when every a in D satisfies R(a,a).
R is irreflexive on domain D when every a in D satisfies NOT R(a,a).
R is functional from its first role when each permitted a relates by R to at most one b within the declared scope.
R is inverse-functional when each permitted b has at most one a related to it by R within scope.
A declared composition R(a,b) AND S(b,c) -> T(a,c); composition is never inferred merely because edges form a path.
A sequence of connected relation instances. A path is evidence of connectivity, not automatically a derived proposition.

guards.reason: Argument reversal requires a symmetric relation or another explicit rule.
A two-edge path does not imply transitivity unless R is declared transitive.
Connectivity does not license a proposition without a declared composition rule.
An inverse relation S need not be the same predicate as R.
Antisymmetry permits both directions when a=b; it is not asymmetry.
Functionality constrains outputs per input; it does not establish inverse functionality.
Observed symmetric instances do not prove the relation is universally symmetric.
A matching example does not establish a universal relation property.
A relation property may be scope/domain constrained.

invariants: Relation arguments are ordered unless the relation semantics explicitly erase that distinction.
A graph path is not automatically an inference.
Transitivity, symmetry, reflexivity, functionality and inverse relationships require declared semantics or separately supported learned rules.
Absence of a relation property declaration means UNKNOWN, not the opposite property.
Relation properties may be scoped to a domain or context.
Observed instances can support a hypothesis about a relation property but cannot promote it to FORMAL_CORE.
Schema-v2 relation catalog declarations may be reused as runtime metadata when compatible, but seed semantics remain versioned and reviewable.
Formal relation inference never grants factual authority or external permission.

provenance.authoring_basis: Standard relation theory and first-order relational properties, adapted to Lantern's conservative typed-graph inference.
